question: An operations manager writes a prompt for a weekly incident summary that the executive team reads every Monday, and a partner firm receives the same summary. Which two elements should the prompt include to make the output usable without rework? Select two.
options: A) A request that the summary be written so that it sounds authoritative and well informed.
B) A note that she is short of time this week and would appreciate a quick turnaround here.
C) The output shape she needs: one page, three headed sections, and no more than six bullets.
D) An instruction telling Claude to use its own judgment about what executives care about.
E) Why customer names must be excluded, since a partner firm also reads it.
correct_answers: C) The output shape she needs: one page, three headed sections, and no more than six bullets.
E) Why customer names must be excluded, since a partner firm also reads it.
explanations: Asking for an authoritative tone shapes how the text sounds, not what it contains, and can encourage confident phrasing over accurate reporting of the week.
Claude's output does not change because the requester is busy. This adds words to the prompt without adding any requirement the draft can be judged against.
Correct. Stating the format and its limits up front is what removes the reformatting step. "One page, three sections, six bullets" is checkable, unlike "keep it short".
Delegating the specification back to Claude is the opposite of describing intent. It guarantees a plausible guess rather than the summary this audience actually needs.
Correct. Giving the reason behind a constraint lets Claude generalise it: knowing an external partner reads the summary, it will also handle account numbers and site names sensibly.
